1009.title: The O Antiphons
1009.hook: from 17 December churches sing O Wisdom, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Emmanuel
1009.howItsDone: In churches that pray evening prayer (Vespers or Evensong), one O antiphon is sung each night in the days before Christmas, before and after the Magnificat; the hymn O come, O come, Emmanuel is sung in Advent in churches of many kinds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Lucy: a crown of candles in the Swedish dark, and a light the darkness doesn't put out. Your line was light in the dark.

O Wisdom. O Root of Jesse. O Key of David. O Emmanuel. Each of these opens a short sung verse, and in the last days before Christmas, churches that pray the evening office sing them one at a time, a new one each night, in monasteries, cathedrals and small parishes. Every verse begins with that one open syllable, O, and every verse ends by asking for the same thing. If you've ever sung the carol O come, O come, Emmanuel, you've already sung versions of these verses, folded together into one hymn.

An antiphon is a short line sung before and after a psalm or canticle, framing it. These ones frame Mary's song, the Magnificat, at evening prayer. Each calls the coming Christ by a name drawn from the old scriptures, several from the prophet Isaiah. Root of Jesse, in the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse, the book of Ruth says, was the father of David. The family tree looks cut down to a stump, and a green shoot pushes up anyway. Key of David is from Isaiah too: "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open." The antiphon asks him to bring out the prisoner who sits in darkness. And Emmanuel comes from Isaiah, taken up by Matthew at the birth of Jesus: "and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." And each ends with a single word: come. Come and teach us. Come and set us free. Come and save us. That's Advent in one syllable. They belong to Catholic Vespers, and Anglicans and Lutherans who keep the evening office sing them too, some in Latin, some in English. The familiar hymn took several and set them to one tune.
screen: `A SHOOT FROM THE STUMP OF JESSE.`
`HE SHALL OPEN, AND NONE SHALL SHUT.`

segments.voice: Let the names go by slowly, Wisdom, Root of Jesse, Key of David, Emmanuel, until one catches: maybe the key, if something in your life feels locked, or the shoot from the stump, if something feels cut down. If you pray, you can say that name with the word that ends every antiphon, O Emmanuel, come; if you don't, hold the picture and breathe with it.
Antiphon. A short line sung before and after a psalm, framing it, as these seven do for Mary's song in the last days before Christmas.
Your line: o come, emmanuel. Old prophecies, with one word underneath. See you on Christmas Eve.

1010.title: Christmas Eve
1010.howItsDone: Churches hold services late on Christmas Eve, some at midnight, often with carols and candles passed from person to person; Catholics celebrate Mass during the night, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil, some of them in January by the older Julian calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the O Antiphons: old names for Christ sung one a night, each ending with come. Your line was o come, emmanuel.

The church lights go down until the building is almost dark. Up front, someone lights a single taper and turns to the person beside them, who tips an unlit candle into the flame. That person turns to the next. The light walks down the rows, hand to hand, until the whole room glows from below, faces lit as if around a campfire. Then everyone starts to sing, softly, a carol the room seems to know by heart. It's late. Some of the children are asleep on their parents' shoulders.

Why at night? Because the story starts at night. Luke puts the first announcement of the birth not in a palace or a temple, but in a field in the dark: "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." Ordinary night-shift workers, awake while everyone else sleeps. An angel appears, the dark lights up, and they are terrified. Then a multitude of angels praises God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." So churches gather late, some at midnight, some earlier for families with small children, to be awake when the shepherds were. Catholic churches celebrate a Mass at night. Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others hold candlelight services, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil in their own way, some in January, by the older calendar. And the carol? Tradition tells it like this. A priest in a small Austrian village wrote some verses in German, Stille Nacht, and asked a local musician to set them to music for the Christmas Eve service. They sang it with a guitar. Some tellings add that the church organ was broken that night, but that detail may have been added later. However it began, the song traveled, and its English words became a Christmas Eve fixture: silent night, holy night. It's an odd thing to call that night silent; in Luke it's full of angels. But the song describes the stillness of a sleeping child, and a world that, for a moment, holds its breath.

Sing a carol, any one you know, even just the first verse under your breath, or hum it, or say the words slowly. Then let it go quiet, and sit in the stillness after it. If you pray, you can let the angels' line be your prayer, glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace; if you don't, just rest in the quiet the song leaves.
Christmas Eve. The night before Christmas, kept with late services and carols by candlelight, because Luke's story begins with shepherds awake in the dark.
Your line: silent night, holy night. The shepherds were awake too. Day one thousand ten, by candlelight.

1011.title: Christmas Day
1011.hook: many Orthodox keep Christmas on 7 January by the old calendar
1011.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the Nativity with services on Christmas Eve or Christmas morning, carols, crib scenes and shared meals; some Orthodox churches keep the feast in January because they follow the older Julian calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas Eve: shepherds awake in a dark field. Your line was silent night, holy night.

Two families, one faith, and two different Christmas mornings. In one house, the feast is today, in December, with the tree and the big meal. In another, the decorations are still waiting, because their church keeps Christmas in January. Some Orthodox churches still count the year by the older Julian calendar, which has drifted out of step with ours. Same feast, same story, same child, on a different page of the calendar. And whichever morning it is, the churches gather around one word for what happened.

Nativity is an old word for a birth, and the Christian calendar uses it for other births too, but on its own it means this one. Luke tells it in a single plain sentence: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." No description of the baby, no speeches. A manger is an animal's feeding trough: the child's first bed was where the animals ate. Churches hear another text alongside it, from Isaiah: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder." Read on Christmas, it sounds like a birth announcement. Christians hear it as fulfilled in Jesus; in Jewish reading, Isaiah is speaking about a king of his own day, and the book was theirs first. Notice the little word us. Not unto the world. Not unto the righteous. Unto us. Read aloud in church on Christmas morning, it sounds as if whoever is listening is being handed the child. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches keep the Nativity, each in its own way. Orthodox icons show the baby in a dark cave, wrapped so tightly some readers see burial bands, as if the end of the story is folded into the beginning. Western churches often set up a crib scene, with ox and donkey, shepherds, and later the magi. Underneath every version is the claim Christians build the feast on: that God came near as a newborn, small enough to be laid in a feeding trough.
screen: `A CAVE, A CRIB, A FEEDING TROUGH.`

segments.voice: Let faces come, family, a neighbor, someone working today while others rest, someone spending the day alone, and stay with one person who might not hear a kind word from anyone else. If you pray, you can hold that person before God with Isaiah's line, unto us a child is born; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.
Nativity. An old word for a birth, and the Christian name for Christmas: the child wrapped and laid in a manger, because there was no room in the inn.
Your line: unto us a child. The us sounds like whoever is listening. Christmas Day, kept.

1012.title: St Stephen (26 December)
1012.hook: the first martyr's day, and Good King Wenceslas carrying food through the snow
1012.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches keep St Stephen's day the day after Christmas, and the Orthodox keep it soon after Christmas on their calendar; in some countries it is a public holiday, and in Britain it is also Boxing Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity: a child laid in a manger, no room in the inn. Your line was unto us a child.

A king stands at his window on a freezing night, the snow deep and crisp and even. Below, a poor man is scraping together sticks for a fire. The king turns to his young servant: who is that, and where does he live? Then he loads up food and drink and firewood, and the two go out into the storm. When the boy can't go on for the cold, the king tells him to step in his footprints, and the ground there is warm. That's the carol Good King Wenceslas, set on the feast of Stephen, the day after Christmas.

In Acts, the new church in Jerusalem had a problem: some of its widows were being left out when the daily food was handed round. So the apostles asked the community to choose men to take charge of the serving, and first on the list, in the King James Bible: "they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost." Stephen's job was food: making sure the women nobody noticed got fed. But he also preached and argued, his words angered the city's council, and in the end they dragged him outside the city and stoned him. Stephen, like the apostles and the people around him, was Jewish; this was a bitter fight inside one community, and Acts tells it that way. His prayers as he dies echo the cross: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then, on his knees: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Acts adds a quiet detail: the men throwing the stones laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who would later become the apostle Paul. Tradition calls Stephen the first martyr. So his feast comes straight after Christmas: the cradle, then the grave. Wenceslas was a real ruler in Bohemia, honored as a saint; the carol is a later story about him. It puts him out in the snow on Stephen's day carrying food to the poor, exactly what Stephen was chosen to do. In some places, the feast became a day for giving to people in need.
screen: `FULL OF FAITH AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`
`LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Think of who might be left out this week, the way those widows were: someone living alone after the holidays, a neighbor who's been sick, a family that's stretched. Hold one of them in mind, and picture the door you'd knock on. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name; if you don't, simply keep them in mind with care.
St Stephen. Chosen in Acts to make sure widows were fed, stoned for his preaching, and remembered by tradition as the first martyr, the day after Christmas.

1013.title: The Holy Innocents (28 December)
1013.hook: the children killed by Herod; a day for all suffering children
1013.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches keep the Holy Innocents a few days after Christmas, and the Orthodox remember them on their own calendar; some churches use the day to pray for children who suffer, and some bless children at the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Stephen: chosen to feed the widows, and the first martyr. Your line was the feast of stephen.

Not every Christmas carol is cheerful. There's an old English one, a lullaby, sung in the voice of the mothers of Bethlehem, rocking their babies and knowing what's coming. Gentle and terrible at once. A few days after Christmas, the church calendar stops the celebration and remembers something nobody would put on a greeting card: the children of Bethlehem killed on the orders of a frightened king. In some churches the vestments turn red, the color worn for martyrs, and in some it has become a day to pray for every child who suffers.

Matthew tells it. Wise men from the east come to King Herod asking where the newborn king of the Jews is. Herod is alarmed. He sends them on to Bethlehem and asks them to report back. They find the child and, warned in a dream, go home another way. Herod "saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth." He orders the children of Bethlehem killed. Joseph, warned in a dream too, has already fled with Mary and the child into Egypt. The child escapes. The others don't. Matthew reaches back to the prophet Jeremiah: "In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Rachel is one of the mothers of Israel, Jacob's beloved wife, and Genesis says she was buried near this very town: "And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem." So Matthew pictures the old mother crying from her grave over the children of her own town. Would not be comforted. The text doesn't hurry her, or explain the deaths, or tidy them up. It lets her grief stand. Tradition calls the Holy Innocents holy not because of anything they did, but because they died, children, in the shadow of the story of Jesus. So the day reaches out to every child caught in someone else's fear and violence, in war, in hunger, in harm at home. Rachel is still weeping, and the day asks the church to weep with her.

Let one suffering child have your attention: a face from the news, a child you know who's having a hard time, or the children of one troubled place. Don't rush to fix the feeling; let it be heavy for a moment, the way Rachel's grief is allowed to be. If you pray, you can hold those children before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind, and stay with them.
Herod. The frightened king whose orders killed the children of Bethlehem, remembered on this quiet day just after Christmas.
Your line: rachel weeping. Her grief is allowed to stand. Gently, until tomorrow.

1014.title: New Year: the Holy Name
1014.hook: on the eighth day he was named Jesus; Catholics also honor Mary, Mother of God
1014.howItsDone: On New Year's Day, Catholics keep the solemnity of Mary, Mother of God; Anglicans and Lutherans keep the Naming and Circumcision of Jesus or the Holy Name; Orthodox Christians keep the Circumcision of the Lord and St Basil's day. Some Christians pray the Jesus Prayer to begin the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod, and Rachel weeping in Bethlehem, her grief allowed to stand. Your line was rachel weeping.

The countdown hits zero, the fireworks go up, and the year turns over. By morning, the new calendar is on the wall with every square still empty. People make resolutions. Some pick a word for the year. The church calendar marks this same day with something older and simpler: a baby being given his name. Count from Christmas, and New Year's Day falls on the eighth day, the day a Jewish boy was circumcised and named. So, in many churches, the calendar year opens with a name.

Luke gives it one verse. In the King James Bible: "And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb." Two things stand out. Mary and Joseph keep the law of their people: Jesus is circumcised and named like any Jewish boy. And they don't choose the name; it was given before he was conceived. Matthew's Gospel says why, in the angel's words to Joseph: "and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." Matthew hears in the name what the child would do. Paul writes to the Philippians that God has "given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." Churches keep this day in different ways. Anglicans and Lutherans keep the Naming and Circumcision of Jesus, or the Holy Name. Orthodox Christians keep the Circumcision of the Lord, along with the memory of St Basil. Catholics keep the feast of Mary, Mother of God, honoring the one who carried the child, and they honor the Holy Name in these early days of January too. In the Orthodox world, a short prayer is built around this name, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Some pray it slowly, with the breath. The church's own year began weeks ago, with Advent. But on the first of January, in many churches, the calendar year starts not with a resolution but with a name, said quietly.
screen: `CIRCUMCISED AND NAMED ON THE EIGHTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can say the name of Jesus quietly on the out-breath, or the Jesus Prayer a line at a time: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. If that isn't your practice, choose one word to carry into the year and say it inside on each breath, and let the empty calendar wait.

1015.title: Epiphany: chalking the door
1015.hook: in some countries families chalk the year and the magi's initials over their door
1015.howItsDone: In Catholic and some Lutheran and Anglican households, families chalk the year and the letters C, M, B over the door around Epiphany, sometimes with chalk blessed at church; in some places a priest visits to bless homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Name, given on the eighth day. Your line was his name was jesus.

Above a front door, in white chalk, there's a short line of numbers, letters and little crosses. The numbers are the new year, split in two at either end. In the middle are three capital letters: C, M, B. It looks like a code, and in a way it is. In parts of Europe, and in Catholic and some Lutheran homes elsewhere, families stand at the door in early January with a stick of chalk, sometimes blessed by a priest, and write it there together. Then it stays, fading slowly, until next year.

Epiphany is the church's word for a showing, an appearing. In Western churches the feast remembers the wise men, the magi, coming to see the child, and through them, the child being shown to the whole world. Matthew tells it: "there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem." Look at what Matthew doesn't say. He doesn't say how many came. He doesn't call them kings or give their names. Tradition counted three, perhaps because of the three gifts, and later named them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. That's the C, the M and the B. There's a second reading of the letters, in Latin: Christus mansionem benedicat. May Christ bless this house. Matthew says where they found the child: "And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." Into the house. Not the manger. In Matthew's telling, the family is in an ordinary home, and strangers from far away are coming through its door. So the chalk marks a front door as a place where Christ has been welcomed, and where guests, and the year itself, will come in. This week ran from the O Antiphons through Christmas Eve, the Nativity, Stephen, the Innocents and the Holy Name. In some Western churches, Epiphany closes the Christmas season, and it ends at a doorway.

Stand at your front door, or picture it clearly, and touch the frame. Think of everyone who comes through it, the people you live with, guests, the neighbor who knocks, and the year that's about to walk in. If you have chalk and want to, you can write the year and the three letters above it. If you pray, you can say the old Latin line's meaning, may Christ bless this house; if you don't, simply wish this doorway well.
Epiphany. A showing: the feast of the wise men finding the child in the house, kept in some homes by chalking the year and C, M, B over the door.
Your line: bless this house. Whoever comes through the door. Day one thousand fifteen.
